extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improv companies and teachers seeking to earn income from workshops, corporate work and events
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for improvisers on generating income: running workshops, teaching, corporate entertainment/training, events and promotions, plus building inclusive companies and getting hired. Covers operational, pedagogical and artistic criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop venue selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose an appropriate space: big, nice and with natural light if possible, but affordable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include dance studios, rehearsal rooms at theatres, arts centres, community centres, church halls or pub function rooms. If dedicated spaces are too expensive, look for cheaper alternatives and 'do a little bit of poking around' to find something that won't break the bank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop pricing and attendance strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Set prices based on local market rates and the quality/length of the workshop; cap attendance and aim to break even.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research other teachers' prices; consider nominal fees for first-time teaching to cover costs. Suggested rule: set an upper limit on attendees (e.g. sixteen) and aim to break even having paid for venue, advertising and expenses with about half that number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop advertising and marketing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple low-cost channels to advertise workshops and attract students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With the Internet, use social networking sites (Facebook, MySpace), and also listings magazines, local papers and printed flyers left in coffee shops, fringe theatres and arts centres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop format: one-off vs series vs drop-in
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to offer single workshops, consecutive series or drop-in sessions, weighing pros and cons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drop-in sessions are hard to teach for mixed-ability groups and attendance can fluctuate; a compromise is periodic beginner workshops plus weekly drop-ins for 'graduates'. Series (e.g. eight-week courses) with prepayment stabilize attendance and finances and allow planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prepaid multi-week courses (The Weekly Shop model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Run multi-week, paid-in-advance courses culminating in performance to ensure regular attendance and predictable finances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An eight-week series paid upfront (with stage-time as a lure) increases regular attendance, allows planning, and can be designed flexibly to meet students' needs. Makes people more likely to show up and lets you plan finances effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streaming and progression of students
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce levels/streams (beginners, intermediate, advanced) and progression paths to grow student body and retain engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example structure: open Level One (eight evenings), Level Two admission by performance, Level Three by invitation where students program their own shows. Streaming lets you take all comers while teaching different ability groups separately; consider moving experienced students into performing company but handle sensitively to avoid turning workshops into auditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid turning workshops into auditions
rubrics_metrics.description: If you charge to teach, keep focus on skill improvement rather than using workshops as auditions for the performing company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you take money to teach people to improvise, ensure the duration of the workshop focuses on helping students improve. Casting from workshops should be handled cautiously to avoid creating the perception of workshops-as-auditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiated teaching for beginners vs experienced performers
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailor teaching to students' needs: beginners need anxiety-reduction and basic technique; experienced players need advanced technique and less work on stage-fright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching inexperienced performers involves both imparting improvisation technique and managing 'being-looked-at-by-strangers' anxiety. Experienced performers require more focus on technique and performance skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leveraging teaching credentials for external work
rubrics_metrics.description: Once established as teachers, offer services to drama schools and societies; adapt improv for acting skills and auditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching improvisation as an acting skill differs from teaching it as an end in itself but can improve actors' responsiveness and audition improvisation. Combine evening classes with paid drama school work to earn a living and recruit performers/helpers from students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate entertainment content selection
rubrics_metrics.description: For corporate audiences, choose fast-moving, crowd-pleasing material; avoid risqué material that can’t be undone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do your easiest, fastest, simplest, most crowd-pleasing stuff. Steer clear of sex and scatology; instead use company in-jokes, client-specific references (software issues, personalities) to get big laughs. Be prepared to infiltrate audience members as characters (waiters, reps) when requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invisible theatre caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Invisible theatre (infiltrating audiences) is often less funny than clients expect, but can be easier than persuading clients to avoid it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These performances rarely match the client's imagined humour, but they can be simpler to execute than convincing a client to back off the idea. Use them judiciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of written sketches as a compromise for clients
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide rehearsed sketches or partly scripted material when clients fear fully unscripted performances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clients sometimes request more control; offering written sketches around which you can improvise gives clients security while allowing performers freedom to adapt if the crowd is failing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate training positioning: Insider vs Outsider
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to present as an 'Insider' who understands the business language or an 'Outsider' offering unique theatre-derived skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insiders study the client's sector and speak its language to gain trust; Outsiders sell what can't be found in the business world and succeed by being different. Choose the approach that fits your team's strengths and target clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measureable outcomes for corporate training
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate intangible skills into measurable outcomes to demonstrate value (e.g., sales figures before/after training).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clients increasingly expect training to be assessed; where possible use objective metrics (sales records, performance indicators) to show improvement post-training, otherwise you risk not getting rehired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliver clear client value in corporate training
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on delivering tangible value; corporate training pays well but requires measurable benefit for the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be focused on the client's objectives and how your methods will deliver them. If there is no detectable improvement, repeat business will dry up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation skills as a training offering
rubrics_metrics.description: Coach businesspeople to perform better in formal presentations by reducing nerves and extracting performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you can coach a nervous improviser or direct an actor, you can coach executives to be more confident and engaging; making the workshop fun can yield big improvements in confidence and skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creativity and brainstorming training
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach techniques for idea generation and running positive brainstorms to overcome fear and ego that stifle corporate creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvisers can model and pass on idea-generation skills; running a constructive brainstorm is achievable for an improv coach with personality and experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teambuilding via improv
rubrics_metrics.description: Use improv exercises to create crisis-based collaboration exercises that build teamwork and cooperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvised performances under time pressure teach cooperation, idea-sharing, and instinctive action. Exercises like 'Arms Through' and 'New Choice' can lower anxiety and create memorable lessons in collaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customer service and sales training using 'yes-and'
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach the 'yes-and' attitude to improve client relationships, sales and customer interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'yes-and' approach is a core improv trait applicable to many business roles; understanding the business is important if positioning as an Insider to make this training effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role-playing and actor-based corporate work
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide role-playing services for training; these can be well-paid but may not utilize comedic skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acting in role-play scenarios for training companies can be profitable and responsibility-light, but offers less room for comedic improvisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting corporate work based on team talents
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursue corporate jobs aligned with the specific talents and interests of your troupe; early jobs tend to define future referrals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The kind of work you get initially will lead to similar opportunities via recommendations. Choose work you can deliver happily and successfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate events and promotions work: scope and cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate events can combine training and entertainment (energizers, motivational speaking, breakout sessions); promotions work often pays poorly and can be degrading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events work may involve assembling elaborate shows or acting as hosts. Promotions (street mascots, handouts) are usually low-paid and humiliating—demand good pay or decline such jobs in favor of building a better reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Getting corporate work: testimonials and partnerships
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain recommendations, testimonials and partner with established providers to get corporate clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most companies hire based on recommendations; collect testimonials, showcase brand-name clients on your website, partner or get introductions from contacts to break into the market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain boundaries: refuse humiliating or low-paid gigs
rubrics_metrics.description: Decline work that involves long hours, terrible costumes, or lots of travel for little money; focus time on reputation-building opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotions work can be humiliating. Be prepared to pass on poorly paid jobs and invest time in building a reputation that leads to better-paid, prouder work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of stage-time as incentive for students
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the promise of stage-time (Micetro shows, end-of-term performances) to encourage sign-up and retention in courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offering performance opportunities at course end motivates students to pay upfront and attend regularly; it also helps create an audience for shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of gender balance and inclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for a healthy gender mix and broader diversity in improv groups and workshops to improve the work and better reflect society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Groups with fairly even gender ratios tend to produce richer, more character- and narrative-based comedy. Actively address female attrition and make workshops welcoming to underrepresented groups (race, sexuality) to better reflect a modern society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding competitive one-upmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not allow competitive gagging that destroys collaboration; improv should prioritize collaboration over individual cleverness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitive games or one-upmanship turn improv into ad-libbed stand-up on a shared stage. To breed collaboration, introduce rules (e.g., first to block loses, tag out anyone who gags at the expense of the story).

rubrics_metrics.name: Countering stereotypical endowing of women on stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent habitual endowing of women into low-status or sexualized roles by training performers to make strong offers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If partners continually assign women PA/secretary roles, women should challenge assumptions with offers like 'I'm the CEO.' Train performers to make strong offers (surgeon, police chief, president) so these become normal in scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to bullying and disrespect
rubrics_metrics.description: If offstage disrespect or onstage bullying occurs, address it; leaving the stage is a last resort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you feel disrespected on stage, recognize nothing binds you to stay; consider leaving as last resort. More productively, work with people you like and who share values; if a group is hostile, start your own with people you respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be truthful rather than merely funny
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritise truthfulness in improvisation because 'truthful things are funnier.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on being truthful and selling good nature; being authentic often produces better comedy than aiming for cleverness alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keith Johnstone's performance fundamentals
rubrics_metrics.description: Core rules from Johnstone: help the other person, give them a good time, don't try to be clever, be obvious and be audible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical exhortations: 'help the other person, to give the other person a good time. Try and give the other improviser what they want. Also don't try to be clever. Be obvious. And be audible.' These guide scene-centric, generous improvisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear vs arrogance: required attitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize fear manifests as arrogance; improvisers should be humble and courageous and 'sell good nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fear often appears as arrogance; aim to look humble and courageous. You can't 'sell good nature' if you're terrified—work to lower anxiety to perform generously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public work should exceed rehearsal quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Hold yourself to a high standard: if your public performances aren't better than rehearsals, there's a problem to solve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure rehearsal work is productive and that public performances confront and solve issues encountered in rehearsal; don't allow public shows to be worse than preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-elimination format improves quality (Micetro observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formats that let the audience eliminate poor performers (e.g., Micetro) can raise standards compared to purely inclusive formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnstone's observation: Micetro is better than Theatresports because the audience can eliminate; improvisation can attract attention-seekers, and competitive elimination can keep standards high.
